title: IGG: A Benchmark for Interactive GUI Grounding under Visibility Constraints

paper.title:
I G G :
A Benchmark for I nteractive G UI G rounding
under Visibility Constraints
paper.abstract:
Abstract GUI grounding benchmarks ask whether an agent can localize a target that is already visible in a static screenshot. Real interfaces often violate this assumption: a target may be off-screen, appear only after a state change or hover, remain occluded, or become actionable after a delay. This leaves the ability to recover target visibility unevaluated.
To measure this reveal step, we introduce Interactive GUI Grounding (IGG) 1 1 1 The benchmark and code are available at https://igg-bench.github.io/ . ,
a benchmark in which an agent must first make the target visible through interaction and then click it.
IGG contains 601 tasks across 16 controllable GUI environments and seven visibility-constraint sub-types, with a compact action space of scrolling, moving, dragging, waiting, and clicking.
In our human study, participants achieve 94.6% accuracy, while GPT-5.5 reaches 79.4% and the strongest evaluated open-source VLM reaches only 31.6%.
To identify the source of this gap, we conduct two controlled interventions. Telling Qwen3-VL which interaction to perform raises its accuracy only from 30.8% to 33.9%, whereas performing the interaction for the model raises it to 81.9%. The bottleneck is executing the reveal interaction, not recognizing the target once it is exposed.
We further show that this capability is learnable,
demonstrating that visibility recovery can be strengthened consistently across model families.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: GUI agents increasingly rely on vision-language models (VLMs) to map natural-language instructions to screen locations Wu et al. (2025) ; Mittal et al. (2026) ; Koh et al. (2024) ; Kumbhar et al. (2026) ; Gao et al. (2024) ; Zheng et al. (2024) . Existing grounding benchmarks evaluate this mapping within a single screenshot and typically assume that the target is already visible Cheng et al. (2024) ; Li et al. (2025) . However, routine interfaces often violate this assumption (Figure 2 ): a target may lie outside the viewport Burigat et al. (2012) , sit in a collapsed panel, be covered by a popup, be distinguishable from its neighbors only on hover, or activate only after a delay. In each case, no static grounding model, however accurate, can localize the target in the initial screenshot. The agent must first select and execute an interaction that reveals it, and only then recognize and click it. Static grounding benchmarks leave this reveal step unmeasured, and navigation benchmarks fold it into end-to-end task success, where it cannot be separated from planning. In light of this gap, this paper asks whether current GUI agents can make a target visible before grounding it and, when they cannot, at which stage they fail. Figure 1: Overview of Interactive GUI Grounding (IGG). Left : representative visibility constraints require observability , disambiguation , state control , or temporal control before the target can be clicked. Center : these capabilities and a compact action space define Viewport Constraint , Multi-State Constraint , and Temporal/Manipulation Constraint . Right : human solvability exceeds model grounding accuracy on all three constraint types, and the gap is largest on viewport constraints for Qwen3-VL and on temporal and manipulation constraints for GPT-5.5. To fill this gap, we introduce Interactive GUI Grounding (IGG) to measure this missing step. An IGG episode decomposes success into four stages: selecting a reveal action , executing it at the correct location or with the correct parameters , recognizing the target once it appears , and localizing the final click . We call the first two stages visibility recovery . The remaining stages, recognizing the target once it appears and localizing the click, coincide with static grounding (Section 3.1 ). Thus, like static grounding, IGG scores a single final click. Unlike static grounding, it additionally requires the agent to recover the target’s visibility beforehand. Because interaction serves only to expose the target, IGG isolates visibility recovery without introducing the broader planning demands of full GUI navigation. IGG contains 601 tasks across 16 controllable GUI environments modeled on familiar applications. Tasks fall into seven sub-types under three constraint types, Viewport , Multi-State , and Temporal/Manipulation , and are solved with five actions: Scroll , Move , Drag , Wait , and Click . Deterministic initial states and stable target identities make evaluation replayable at click time, while the environments preserve the interaction patterns that make visibility recovery difficult: hover reveals, popups, delayed activation, carousels, and movable occlusions. Our experiments identify interaction execution as the main bottleneck in IGG. Telling a model which interaction to perform provides little improvement, whereas performing the reveal action for it recovers most of its accuracy. SFT on successful interaction trajectories followed by online GRPO further improves visibility recovery across Qwen3-VL, InternVL3.5, and GUI-Owl-1.5. Our contributions are: • We formulate interactive GUI grounding as visibility recovery followed by target recognition and localization, separating it from both static grounding and end-to-end navigation. • We introduce IGG, a benchmark of 601 tasks, 16 controllable GUI environments, and seven visibility-constraint sub-types, together with a click-time evaluator and human-verified ground-truth interaction trajectories. • We provide controlled interventions, heuristic analyses, cross-viewport and paired mock-real evaluations, and training studies that identify where current agents fail and show consistent improvements across three VLM architectures.

sections.heading: GUI grounding.
sections.text: GUI grounding maps a natural-language instruction to the corresponding interface element ( Cheng et al., 2024 ; Tang et al., 2025 ) . ScreenSpot ( Cheng et al., 2024 ) , ScreenSpot-Pro ( Li et al., 2025 ) , and OSWorld-G ( Xie et al., 2025 ) evaluate localization within a screenshot where the target is visible. Recent methods improve this setting through rich screenshot supervision ( Gao et al., 2024 ) , diffusion-based prediction ( Kumbhar et al., 2026 ) , UI decomposition ( Xie et al., 2025 ) , and multi-turn refinement ( Mittal et al., 2026 ) . Universal grounding extends localization to agent settings ( Gou et al., 2025 ) , but still predicts a target from the currently observed state. IGG instead evaluates the preceding visibility-recovery step: the agent must change the interface before the target can be recognized and localized.

sections.heading: GUI navigation
sections.text: Mind2Web ( Deng et al., 2023 ) , WebArena ( Zhou et al., 2024 ) , OSWorld ( Xie et al., 2024 ) evaluate multi-step task completion on web and desktop interfaces, and agent-side improvements such as interaction-history compression ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) are measured against their end-to-end success. Because only end-to-end success is scored, planning, exploration, and grounding failures collapse into a single signal. IGG instead scores one narrower capability, visibility recovery followed by a single evaluated click (Section 3.1 ). Just as static grounding was separated from navigation and became a standard evaluation axis ( Cheng et al., 2024 ) , IGG isolates a step that navigation benchmarks contain only implicitly, and it complements rather than replaces them.

sections.heading: 3 The IGG Benchmark
sections.text: Our goal is to measure visibility recovery in isolation and reproducibly. To this end, we formalize the task (Section 3.1 ), categorize the interactions it requires (Section 3.2 ), describe the environments and how tasks were built (Section 3.3 ), specify the evaluation protocol (Section 4.1 ), and validate the benchmark with human studies (Section 4.5 ).

sections.heading: 3.1 Problem formulation
sections.text: An IGG task is specified by an initial interface state in which the target is not visible or not actionable, a goal-only instruction q q that identifies the target but not the procedure for exposing it, a target element with a stable identifier, and an evaluator that scores a Click as successful if and only if the clicked element’s identifier matches the target’s. Each task also carries one human-verified ground-truth trace, which is withheld from the agent and used only for efficiency metrics. At step t t , the agent receives the screenshot s t s_{t} , the instruction q q , and its action history h t − 1 = ( a 1 , … , a t − 1 ) h_{t-1}=(a_{1},\ldots,a_{t-1}) , selects an action from 𝒜 = { Scroll , Move , Drag , Wait , Click } , \mathcal{A}=\{\textsc{Scroll},\textsc{Move},\textsc{Drag},\textsc{Wait},\textsc{Click}\}, and receives the next screenshot s t + 1 s_{t+1} (Table 1 ). IGG uses screenshot-only observations and restricts interaction to these five reveal-and-click actions. The episode ends with success on the first click that hits the target and with failure when the action budget is exhausted. A click elsewhere applies any defined state transition, and the episode continues. sections.heading: 3.2 Visibility constraint taxonomy
sections.text: We categorize tasks by the interaction required to recover target visibility (Figures 1 and 2 ).

sections.heading: Constraint Type 1: Viewport Constraint.
sections.text: The target is outside the current viewport but reachable within the same UI state. • CT1-1. Scroll-based Exploration: The target is off-screen and must be revealed by scrolling within the current state.

sections.heading: Constraint Type 2: Multi-State Constraint.
sections.text: The target, or the visual cue needed to identify it, is hidden by the current UI state and must be revealed through a state-changing interaction. • CT2-1. Visual Disambiguation: The target is visually similar to other elements and can only be distinguished through hover-based cues such as tooltips or labels, requiring a Move before the final Click . • CT2-2. Hidden State Activation: The target is contained in a collapsed or inactive UI region, such as a dropdown, tab, or side panel, that must be opened before clicking. • CT2-3. Removable Occlusion: A blocking element, such as a popup or modal, hides the target and must be dismissed before the target can be clicked.

sections.heading: Constraint Type 3: Temporal & Manipulation Constraint.
sections.text: Reaching the target requires temporal control or spatial manipulation. • CT3-1. Delayed State Activation: The target is initially inactive and becomes interactable only after a temporal delay or asynchronous event, requiring a Wait before clicking. • CT3-2. Dynamic Target Interaction: The target resides in an automatically transitioning element, such as a carousel or ticker, and must be reached by waiting for the correct state or by using navigation controls. • CT3-3. Movable Occlusion: A UI element occludes the target due to its position or size, requiring a Drag to reposition or resize the occluding element.

sections.heading: 3.3 Environments and task construction
sections.text: Figure 3: Distribution of IGG tasks. (a) Task distribution across the three constraint types and their sub-types. (b) Number of tasks per platform, broken down by sub-type. We want environments that are deterministic enough to score a click programmatically, yet rich enough in interaction to make visibility recovery difficult. IGG comprises 601 tasks across 16 controllable environments modeled on widely used applications such as Gmail, Google Calendar, VS Code, Figma, Spotify, and YouTube (full list in Appendix A ). 2 2 2 Real applications are named as canonical references only, and no affiliation with or endorsement by their owners is implied. Each environment is a deterministic web application: every task starts from a fixed initial state, state transitions are reproducible, and every element carries a stable identifier, so the evaluator decides success at click time without heuristic matching. At the same time, the environments implement the interaction patterns that visibility recovery requires, including hover reveals, collapsible panels, popups, delayed activation, carousels, and draggable occluders. Tasks are built in three steps. A multimodal agent first drafts a goal-only instruction and a reference trace for each target. Annotators then rewrite instructions that leak the procedure (“Click ‘Reply’ on Minji’s message” rather than “Hover over the message and click ‘Reply’ ”, as in Figure A10 ) and add a natural disambiguating cue, such as an author, title, or surrounding content, when several elements share a label (Appendix C.3 ). Finally, annotators replay every trace to confirm that the target is unique and reachable. Figure 3 shows the resulting distribution over sub-types and environments.

sections.heading: 4.1 Evaluation setup
sections.text: IGG combines task specifications, 16 controllable GUI environments, and a Playwright-driven Chromium evaluator at a × 900 1440\!\times\!900 viewport. On each CLICK , the evaluator compares the clicked element ID with the target ID; a match ends the episode, while a mismatch returns the updated screenshot. Models receive only screenshots, the goal-only instruction, and action history. The DOM, accessibility tree, target ID, and ground-truth interaction trajectory remain hidden. Each baseline is evaluated once per task after an environment reset; main runs use an eight-action budget and greedy decoding unless noted. Table D provides the prompts, decoding settings, and action formats.

sections.heading: 4.3 Where does interactive grounding fail?
sections.text: We intervene at two points in the four-stage decomposition from Section 3.1 . In the first condition, the model is told which reveal interaction is required but must determine its location and parameters. In the second, we perform the ground-truth reveal trajectory and ask the model only for the final click. Table 4: Grounding accuracy (%) when a model solves the complete task, is told the required interaction, or receives the interface after the reveal interaction has been performed. Condition Qwen3-VL GPT-5.4 Mini (Low) Full task 30.8 72.4 Interaction specified 33.9 – Reveal performed 81.9 90.4 Naming the interaction changes Qwen3-VL by only 3.1 points, whereas completing it raises accuracy by 51.1 points. Providing the correct reveal-action category is therefore insufficient. Most remaining errors arise from choosing its location or parameters and executing the reveal correctly, before target recognition and final-click localization are evaluated. Target-agnostic heuristics further separate easy and hard reveal patterns (Appendix F.3 ). Fixed scrolling, hovering, and waiting reveal 68.8%, 61.4%, and 87.1% of their matched tasks, whereas popup dismissal and occluder dragging reach 17.6% and 16.9%. The difficult cases require identifying which element controls visibility and how to manipulate it. Failed Qwen3-VL trajectories show the same pattern. When the ground-truth trajectory requires Drag , Scroll , or Move , failed runs omit that action in 59/59, 207/247, and 71/96 cases, respectively (Appendix F.2 ). This motivates first expanding the policy’s action support with SFT, then improving execution with online feedback.

sections.heading: 4.4 Learning missing interaction priors
sections.text: We ask whether training can supply reveal actions that base VLMs rarely use. Drag provides the clearest case: Qwen2.5-VL, Qwen3-VL, and GUI-Owl-1.5 emit no drag actions on the held-out tasks.

sections.heading: Setup.
sections.text: After excluding two tasks whose ground-truth trajectories could not be replayed reliably, we use 479 tasks for training and reserve 120 for evaluation. The held-out tasks contribute neither SFT examples nor GRPO rollouts.

sections.heading: Supervised training on successful trajectories Hu et al. (2022) .
sections.text: We fine-tune the model on human-verified successful trajectories. Let x t x_{t} denote the instruction, screenshot, and interaction history at step t t , and let a t a_{t} be the next ground-truth action. We optimize a weighted next-action negative log-likelihood Pomerleau (1991) : ℒ SFT ​ ( θ ) = − E ( x t , a t ) ∼ 𝒟 ​ [ w ⁡ ( a t ) ​ log ⁡ π θ ​ ( a t ∣ x t ) ] . \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SFT}}(\theta)=-\mathrm{E}_{(x_{t},a_{t})\sim\mathcal{D}}\left[w(a_{t})\log\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid x_{t})\right]. For standard behavior cloning, w ⁡ ( a t ) = 1 w(a_{t})=1 . In the frequency-balanced variant Cui et al. (2019) , we increase w ⁡ ( a t ) w(a_{t}) for rare reveal actions such as Move , Wait , and Drag ; details are in Appendix G . The model still receives goal-only instructions. Only the training distribution changes.

sections.heading: Refining interactions with online feedback Shao et al. (2024) .
sections.text: We then apply online GRPO under the same eight-action interaction budget as main evaluation. The reward is defined over browser-executed trajectories rather than text strings: R ⁡ ( τ ) = R out ​ ( τ ) + R proc ​ ( τ ) − λ step ​ | τ | − R err ​ ( τ ) . R(\tau)=R_{\mathrm{out}}(\tau)+R_{\mathrm{proc}}(\tau)-\lambda_{\mathrm{step}}|\tau|-R_{\mathrm{err}}(\tau). R out R_{\mathrm{out}} rewards click-time target success, R proc R_{\mathrm{proc}} gives bounded credit for visibility-changing progress, and R err R_{\mathrm{err}} penalizes wrong clicks, empty clicks, invalid actions, and repeated ineffective actions. Exact weights and optimization hyperparameters are provided in Appendix G . The two stages serve different roles. SFT broadens action support, after which GRPO selects among those actions using online feedback. If a seed policy never samples Drag , GRPO observes no successful drag rollout to reinforce. Frequency-balanced SFT brings rare reveal actions into the policy’s sampled support, enabling GRPO to optimize their selection and execution.

sections.heading: Results.
sections.text: The two-stage procedure raises Qwen3-VL from 40.0% to 59.2% GA (Figure 6 ). On Movable Occlusion, frequency-balanced SFT emits Drag in 7/8 required-drag tasks and solves 4/8; GRPO raises this to 5/8. Initialization also matters on Dynamic Target Interaction: GRPO reaches 60.0% from the frequency-balanced seed but 30.0% from the standard SFT seed. The same procedure improves InternVL3.5 from 28.3% to 47.5% and GUI-Owl-1.5 from 35.0% to 52.5% (Table A8 ), showing consistent gains across three architectures. The best trained model improves Qwen3-VL from 40.0% to 59.2% GA on the 120-task validation split. Baseline VLMs solve some validation tasks without emitting every action in the ground-truth trajectory, but emit no drag actions. SFT introduces these actions into the policy’s support, after which GRPO improves task success. (a) Action share across GRPO variants. (b) Validation GA across GRPO checkpoints. The frequency-balanced seed gives the policy access to rare reveal actions, after which online reward improves their selection and execution. sections.heading: 4.5 Human solvability and environment fidelity
sections.text: A failure on IGG is informative only if the task is solvable and the environment is faithful to the interface it models. Before comparing models, we therefore verify both with the same 15 participants (protocol details in Appendix H ).

sections.heading: Task solvability.
sections.text: Participants solve a fixed suite of 21 tasks, three from each sub-type, using the same instructions and interfaces given to the models, without the constraint label, target ID, target coordinates, or reveal procedure. A trial ends on the correct target click or after eight click-or-drag attempts. Scrolling and hovering are recorded but do not count, so the limit is comparable to, though not identical with, the eight-action model budget. Participants succeed in 298 of 315 trials (94.6%) with a mean completion time of 19.8 seconds (Table 5 ). Together with the replay verification of every reference trace, this indicates that the model failures reported below do not stem from unsolvable tasks or ambiguous instructions.

sections.heading: Environment fidelity.
sections.text: The same participants compare seven representative environments with their real-interface counterparts and rate visual realism, interaction realism, and task executability on five-point scales, giving mean scores of 4.50, 4.64, and 4.75 (Table 6 ). Appendix C.2 complements these ratings with visual-similarity metrics and a preliminary paired mock–real evaluation on 16 tasks, one per environment, in which model ordering is preserved across the two settings and the Qwen3-VL model trained in Section 4.4 leads in both.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced IGG to make visibility recovery a measurable component of GUI grounding. Our analyses show that knowing which interaction is required is not enough; current models most often fail in deciding where and how to carry it out. Training on successful interaction trajectories followed by online feedback improves this capability consistently across model families. IGG therefore provides a focused setting for evaluating and learning the interactions that must precede a grounding click.

sections.heading: 6 Limitations
sections.text: IGG uses deterministic mockups for controlled and reproducible evaluation. Our fidelity analyses, including paired mock-real evaluation, suggest that these environments capture relevant visual and interaction patterns, but they do not replace evaluation on live interfaces. Interactive grounding can support accessibility and UI testing, but the same capability may also be misused for automated interaction. We therefore release only controlled mockups that are not connected to external services.

sections.heading: B.1 Viewport robustness
sections.text: The main benchmark fixes the viewport at 1440 × 900 1440\times 900 so that initial target visibility and constraint type remain constant across models. Responsive layouts can change whether a target is hidden and which interaction reveals it, so the viewport is part of the task specification. To test whether the learned behavior depends on this layout, we regenerate the 601 tasks at five viewport sizes corresponding to desktop, mobile portrait, tablet, split-screen, and zoomed displays, and keep the 127 tasks that remain valid in every layout (i.e., the target is initially hidden and the reference trace replays successfully). The subset contains 103 training and 24 held-out tasks, so the study measures whether behavior learned at 1440 × 900 1440\times 900 survives a layout change rather than held-out generalization. On this subset, the trained Qwen3-VL model outperforms its base model by 11.1-17.3 points at every viewport, including mobile portrait (Table A2 ). sections.heading: C.2 Mockup fidelity
sections.text: Each task starts from a resettable state, executes deterministic transitions, and uses a stable target ID for click-time evaluation. The environments implement the visibility-changing interactions measured by IGG, including hidden panels, hover reveals, popups, delayed elements, carousels, and movable occlusions. We evaluate their fidelity to real-interface counterparts using visual similarity, human ratings, and paired task execution.

sections.heading: Visual similarity.
sections.text: We measure visual similarity between each mockup and its corresponding real-application reference listed in Table A1 . sections.heading: C.3 Instruction design
sections.text: Instructions name the target but not the reveal procedure. Annotators avoid action hints such as “scroll down,” “hover over the icon,” or “wait until the button appears,” and add a natural cue, such as an author, document title, or surrounding content, when several elements share a label. For example, “Scroll down and click Kai” becomes “Find Kai in the direct message list,” and “Drag the sticky note away and click QA Checklist” becomes “Click the QA Checklist note without deleting any notes.” Multimodal LLMs propose candidate instructions and reference traces, and annotators correct the wording, repair traces where needed, and replay every task to verify that the target is unique and reachable.

sections.heading: Effect of procedural hints.
sections.text: As a diagnostic, we also evaluate instructions that state the intermediate procedure. Unlike the reveal action given condition of Section 4.3 , which names only the action type, these hints describe the procedure. With such hints, Qwen3-VL rises from 30.8% to 56.9% GA over all 601 tasks, but hints do not solve precise manipulation: hinted Qwen3-VL solves 0 of 8 held-out movable-occlusion tasks, whereas SFT+GRPO solves 5 of 8 without any test-time hint. The main benchmark therefore retains goal-only instructions, and the training gains reflect an executable interaction prior rather than instruction following.

sections.heading: Appendix D Evaluation Protocol
sections.text: The open-source baselines are Qwen/Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct , Qwen/Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct , and mPLUG/GUI-Owl-1.5-8B-Instruct , and the commercial baseline is gpt-5.5 . Each model is evaluated once per task with greedy decoding from a reset environment. At each turn, the agent receives the system prompt, task instruction, screenshot, step index, coordinate space, and action history. It returns one JSON action. Otherwise the environment applies any defined state transition and returns the next screenshot. Navigation outside the task environment is disabled, and the episode ends on success or budget exhaustion. In that case, take the minimum interaction needed to reveal it (scroll, hover, expand, wait, drag away an occluder, etc.) and then click the element. This is a grounding task, not a navigation task. Do NOT try to complete any higher-level workflow; just find the target and click it. ... Action space (emit exactly ONE action per turn): - Scroll a region: {"type": "scroll", "x": <int>, "y": <int>, "dy": <int>} dy > 0 scrolls down, dy < 0 scrolls up. Use (x, y) to pick which scroll container gets the event (e.g. a left sidebar vs the main feed). - Move the cursor: {"type": "move", "x": <int>, "y": <int>} Triggers hover effects, tooltips, and hover-reveal menus. - Drag: {"type": "drag", "startX": <int>, "startY": <int>, "endX": <int>, "endY": <int>} Use to nudge an occluding popup aside without fully closing it, or to move sliders/panels. - Wait: {"type": "wait", "ms": <int>} Use when the target is gated by a timer, async load, ad countdown, auto-rotating carousel, etc. - Click: {"type": "click", "x": <int>, "y": <int>} Grounding trigger. Identify a unique visual description of the target. 2. Scan the screenshot. If the target is visible, click its center. 3. If not visible, reason about why: is it offscreen, in a collapsed panel, hidden behind a popup, revealed only on hover, or not loaded yet? 4. Pick the single cheapest action that could make it visible or confirm it. 5. Avoid exploratory clicks on random UI elements; each click is evaluated. Output format (STRICT): Reply with exactly ONE line containing a single JSON object for the next action. No prose, no markdown, no code fences, no explanation. sections.heading: Appendix G Training Details
sections.text: Our two-stage procedure uses SFT to introduce rare reveal actions and online GRPO to optimize their execution from browser feedback.

sections.heading: G.1 Training Setup
sections.text: Two tasks whose ground-truth trajectories could not be replayed reliably during corpus construction are excluded before splitting the remaining 599 tasks into 479 training tasks and 120 held-out validation tasks. Every included ground-truth trajectory is human-corrected and verified by replay; validation tasks contribute neither SFT examples nor GRPO rollouts.

sections.heading: G.2 SFT
sections.text: The ground-truth trajectories yield 1,141 action-level examples with normalized coordinates. We use LoRA rank 8, alpha 32, dropout 0.05, all-linear language-model target modules, a frozen vision tower and projector, bf16, learning rate 1 × 10 − 4 1\times 10^{-4} , effective batch size 8, maximum length 8192, maximum image pixels 1,382,400, and 500 steps with checkpoints every 100 steps. Frequency balancing oversamples Click / Scroll / Move / Wait / Drag by 1/1/2/2/4, expanding the data to 1,460 examples and the drag examples from 55 to 220.

sections.heading: G.3 Online GRPO
sections.text: GRPO starts from an SFT LoRA seed and collects online browser rollouts from the 479 training tasks under the same eight-action budget used in evaluation. We use group size 6, temperature 1.0, top- p p 0.95 for rollout sampling, learning rate 2 × 10 − 6 2\times 10^{-6} , PPO-style clipping with ϵ = 0.2 \epsilon=0.2 , maximum gradient norm 1.0, and up to 20 update groups. We evaluate saved LoRA checkpoints with greedy decoding on the fixed 120-task validation split.

sections.heading: Online interaction reward.
sections.text: The reward is computed from browser-executed traces. Let S S denote target-click success; T T the action count; W W non-empty wrong clicks; E E empty clicks; I I invalid actions; A A repeated ineffective actions; and R R repeated wrong-click locations. The bounded bonus B B rewards reveal progress (Table A9 ). Successful traces with prior wrong clicks are capped at 1.2, shortcut successes at 0.8, and runtime or parsing failures are excluded from policy updates.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.32536v1 [cs.AI] 23 Oct 2026 I G G : A Benchmark for I nteractive G UI G rounding under Visibility Constraints Kyeongseon Kim Affiliation: KAIST Correspondence: ella94.ai@gmail.com Jiyeon Son Affiliation: KAIST Correspondence: ella94.ai@gmail.com Tae-Hyun Oh Affiliation: KAIST Correspondence: ella94.ai@gmail.com Abstract GUI grounding benchmarks ask whether an agent can localize a target that is already visible in a static screenshot. Real interfaces often violate this assumption: a target may be off-screen, appear only after a state change or hover, remain occluded, or become actionable after a delay. This leaves the ability to recover target visibility unevaluated. To measure this reveal step, we introduce Interactive GUI Grounding (IGG) 1 1 1 The benchmark and code are available at https://igg-bench.github.io/ . , a benchmark in which an agent must first make the target visible through interaction and then click it. IGG contains 601 tasks across 16 controllable GUI environments and seven visibility-constraint sub-types, with a compact action space of scrolling, moving, dragging, waiting, and clicking. In our human study, participants achieve 94.6% accuracy, while GPT-5.5 reaches 79.4% and the strongest evaluated open-source VLM reaches only 31.6%. To identify the source of this gap, we conduct two controlled interventions. Telling Qwen3-VL which interaction to perform raises its accuracy only from 30.8% to 33.9%, whereas performing the interaction for the model raises it to 81.9%. The bottleneck is executing the reveal interaction, not recognizing the target once it is exposed. We further show that this capability is learnable, demonstrating that visibility recovery can be strengthened consistently across model families. † † footnotetext: * Equal contribution. 1 Introduction GUI agents increasingly rely on vision-language models (VLMs) to map natural-language instructions to screen locations Wu et al. (2025) ; Mittal et al. (2026) ; Koh et al. (2024) ; Kumbhar et al. (2026) ; Gao et al. (2024) ; Zheng et al. (2024) . Existing grounding benchmarks evaluate this mapping within a single screenshot and typically assume that the target is already visible Cheng et al. (2024) ; Li et al. (2025) . However, routine interfaces often violate this assumption (Figure 2 ): a target may lie outside the viewport Burigat et al. (2012) , sit in a collapsed panel, be covered by a popup, be distinguishable from its neighbors only on hover, or activate only after a delay. In each case, no static grounding model, however accurate, can localize the target in the initial screenshot. The agent must first select and execute an interaction that reveals it, and only then recognize and click it. Static grounding benchmarks leave this reveal step unmeasured, and navigation benchmarks fold it into end-to-end task success, where it cannot be separated from planning. In light of this gap, this paper asks whether current GUI agents can make a target visible before grounding it and, when they cannot, at which stage they fail. Figure 1: Overview of Interactive GUI Grounding (IGG). Left : representative visibility constraints require observability , disambiguation , state control , or temporal control before the target can be clicked. Center : these capabilities and a compact action space define Viewport Constraint , Multi-State Constraint , and Temporal/Manipulation Constraint . Right : human solvability exceeds model grounding accuracy on all three constraint types, and the gap is largest on viewport constraints for Qwen3-VL and on temporal and manipulation constraints for GPT-5.5. To fill this gap, we introduce Interactive GUI Grounding (IGG) to measure this missing step. An IGG episode decomposes success into four stages: selecting a reveal action , executing it at the correct location or with the correct parameters , recognizing the target once it appears , and localizing the final click . We call the first two stages visibility recovery . The remaining stages, recognizing the target once it appears and localizing the click, coincide with static grounding (Section 3.1 ). Thus, like static grounding, IGG scores a single final click. Unlike static grounding, it additionally requires the agent to recover the target’s visibility beforehand. Because interaction serves only to expose the target, IGG isolates visibility recovery without introducing the broader planning demands of full GUI navigation. IGG contains 601 tasks across 16 controllable GUI environments modeled on familiar applications. Tasks fall into seven sub-types under three constraint types, Viewport , Multi-State , and Temporal/Manipulation , and are solved with five actions: Scroll , Move , Drag , Wait , and Click . Deterministic initial states and stable target identities make evaluation replayable at click time, while the environments preserve the interaction patterns that make visibility recovery difficult: hover reveals, popups, delayed activation, carousels, and movable occlusions. Our experiments identify interaction execution as the main bottleneck in IGG. Telling a model which interaction to perform provides little improvement, whereas performing the reveal action for it recovers most of its accuracy. SFT on successful interaction trajectories followed by online GRPO further improves visibility recovery across Qwen3-VL, InternVL3.5, and GUI-Owl-1.5. Our contributions are: • We formulate interactive GUI grounding as visibility recovery followed by target recognition and localization, separating it from both static grounding and end-to-end navigation. • We introduce IGG, a benchmark of 601 tasks, 16 controllable GUI environments, and seven visibility-constraint sub-types, together with a click-time evaluator and human-verified ground-truth interaction trajectories. • We provide controlled interventions, heuristic analyses, cross-viewport and paired mock-real evaluations, and training studies that identify where current agents fail and show consistent improvements across three VLM architectures. 2 Related Work GUI grounding. GUI grounding maps a natural-language instruction to the corresponding interface element ( Cheng et al., 2024 ; Tang et al., 2025 ) . ScreenSpot ( Cheng et al., 2024 ) , ScreenSpot-Pro ( Li et al., 2025 ) , and OSWorld-G ( Xie et al., 2025 ) evaluate localization within a screenshot where the target is visible. Recent methods improve this setting through rich screenshot supervision ( Gao et al., 2024 ) , diffusion-based prediction ( Kumbhar et al., 2026 ) , UI decomposition ( Xie et al., 2025 ) , and multi-turn refinement ( Mittal et al., 2026 ) . Universal grounding extends localization to agent settings ( Gou et al., 2025 ) , but still predicts a target from the currently observed state. IGG instead evaluates the preceding visibility-recovery step: the agent must change the interface before the target can be recognized and localized. GUI navigation Mind2Web ( Deng et al., 2023 ) , WebArena ( Zhou et al., 2024 ) , OSWorld ( Xie et al., 2024 ) evaluate multi-step task completion on web and desktop interfaces, and agent-side improvements such as interaction-history compression ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) are measured against their end-to-end success. Because only end-to-end success is scored, planning, exploration, and grounding failures collapse into a single signal. IGG instead scores one narrower capability, visibility recovery followed by a single evaluated click (Section 3.1 ). Just as static grounding was separated from navigation and became a standard evaluation axis ( Cheng et al., 2024 ) , IGG isolates a step that navigation benchmarks contain only implicitly, and it complements rather than replaces them. 3 The IGG Benchmark Our goal is to measure visibility recovery in isolation and reproducibly. To this end, we formalize the task (Section 3.1 ), categorize the interactions it requires (Section 3.2 ), describe the environments and how tasks were built (Section 3.3 ), specify the evaluation protocol (Section 4.1 ), and validate the benchmark with human studies (Section 4.5 ). 3.1 Problem formulation An IGG task is specified by an initial interface state in which the target is not visible or not actionable, a goal-only instruction q q that identifies the target but not the procedure for exposing it, a target element with a stable identifier, and an evaluator that scores a Click as successful if and only if the clicked element’s identifier matches the target’s. Each task also carries one human-verified ground-truth trace, which is withheld from the agent and used only for efficiency metrics. At step t t , the agent receives the screenshot s t s_{t} , the instruction q q , and its action history h t − 1 = ( a 1 , … , a t − 1 ) h_{t-1}=(a_{1},\ldots,a_{t-1}) , selects an action from 𝒜 = { Scroll , Move , Drag , Wait , Click } , \mathcal{A}=\{\textsc{Scroll},\textsc{Move},\textsc{Drag},\textsc{Wait},\textsc{Click}\}, and receives the next screenshot s t + 1 s_{t+1} (Table 1 ). IGG uses screenshot-only observations and restricts interaction to these five reveal-and-click actions. The episode ends with success on the first click that hits the target and with failure when the action budget is exhausted. A click elsewhere applies any defined state transition, and the episode continues. Figure 2: Examples of the three IGG constraint types: viewport, multi-state, and temporal or manipulation constraints. Additional examples appear in Appendix E.2 . Table 1: Minimal action space 𝒜 \mathcal{A} for visibility recovery. Action Role SCROLL ( dir , Δ px ) (\mathrm{dir},\Delta_{\mathrm{px}}) Scroll to reveal off-screen regions. MOVE ( x px , y px ) (x_{\mathrm{px}},y_{\mathrm{px}}) Move the pointer to trigger hover states or expose disambiguating cues. DRAG ( startX , startY , endX , endY ) Drag an element between the specified start and end coordinates. Constraint Type 1: Viewport Constraint. The target is outside the current viewport but reachable within the same UI state. • CT1-1. Scroll-based Exploration: The target is off-screen and must be revealed by scrolling within the current state. Constraint Type 2: Multi-State Constraint. The target, or the visual cue needed to identify it, is hidden by the current UI state and must be revealed through a state-changing interaction. • CT2-1. Visual Disambiguation: The target is visually similar to other elements and can only be distinguished through hover-based cues such as tooltips or labels, requiring a Move before the final Click . • CT2-2. Hidden State Activation: The target is contained in a collapsed or inactive UI region, such as a dropdown, tab, or side panel, that must be opened before clicking. • CT2-3. Removable Occlusion: A blocking element, such as a popup or modal, hides the target and must be dismissed before the target can be clicked. Constraint Type 3: Temporal & Manipulation Constraint. Reaching the target requires temporal control or spatial manipulation. • CT3-1. Delayed State Activation: The target is initially inactive and becomes interactable only after a temporal delay or asynchronous event, requiring a Wait before clicking. • CT3-2. Dynamic Target Interaction: The target resides in an automatically transitioning element, such as a carousel or ticker, and must be reached by waiting for the correct state or by using navigation controls. • CT3-3. Movable Occlusion: A UI element occludes the target due to its position or size, requiring a Drag to reposition or resize the occluding element. 3.3 Environments and task construction Figure 3: Distribution of IGG tasks. (a) Task distribution across the three constraint types and their sub-types. (b) Number of tasks per platform, broken down by sub-type. We want environments that are deterministic enough to score a click programmatically, yet rich enough in interaction to make visibility recovery difficult. IGG comprises 601 tasks across 16 controllable environments modeled on widely used applications such as Gmail, Google Calendar, VS Code, Figma, Spotify, and YouTube (full list in Appendix A ). 2 2 2 Real applications are named as canonical references only, and no affiliation with or endorsement by their owners is implied. Each environment is a deterministic web application: every task starts from a fixed initial state, state transitions are reproducible, and every element carries a stable identifier, so the evaluator decides success at click time without heuristic matching. At the same time, the environments implement the interaction patterns that visibility recovery requires, including hover reveals, collapsible panels, popups, delayed activation, carousels, and draggable occluders. Tasks are built in three steps. A multimodal agent first drafts a goal-only instruction and a reference trace for each target. Annotators then rewrite instructions that leak the procedure (“Click ‘Reply’ on Minji’s message” rather than “Hover over the message and click ‘Reply’ ”, as in Figure A10 ) and add a natural disambiguating cue, such as an author, title, or surrounding content, when several elements share a label (Appendix C.3 ). Finally, annotators replay every trace to confirm that the target is unique and reachable. Figure 3 shows the resulting distribution over sub-types and environments. 4 Evaluation and Experiments 4.1 Evaluation setup IGG combines task specifications, 16 controllable GUI environments, and a Playwright-driven Chromium evaluator at a × 900 1440\!\times\!900 viewport. On each CLICK , the evaluator compares the clicked element ID with the target ID; a match ends the episode, while a mismatch returns the updated screenshot. Models receive only screenshots, the goal-only instruction, and action history. The DOM, accessibility tree, target ID, and ground-truth interaction trajectory remain hidden. Each baseline is evaluated once per task after an environment reset; main runs use an eight-action budget and greedy decoding unless noted. Table D provides the prompts, decoding settings, and action formats. Metrics. We report the following metrics: • Grounding Accuracy (GA) ↑ \uparrow : the fraction of tasks in which the agent clicks the target element within the action budget. • Action Cost (AC) ↓ \downarrow : mean number of actions executed until success or budget exhaustion. • Reference Efficiency Ratio (RER) ↑ \uparrow : mean of | g i | / | a i | |g_{i}|/|a_{i}| over successful tasks, where g i g_{i} is the annotated ground-truth trajectory and a i a_{i} is the agent trajectory; values above 1 indicate trajectories shorter than the annotated ground-truth trajectory. • Total Time (TT) ↓ \downarrow : mean elapsed wall-clock time per task. GA measures success; AC and RER measure interaction efficiency. TT is reported descriptively: local and API-backed models use different serving stacks, so their runtimes are not hardware-normalized. We intervene at two points in the four-stage decomposition from Section 3.1 . In the first condition, the model is told which reveal interaction is required but must determine its location and parameters. In the second, we perform the ground-truth reveal trajectory and ask the model only for the final click. Table 4: Grounding accuracy (%) when a model solves the complete task, is told the required interaction, or receives the interface after the reveal interaction has been performed. Condition Qwen3-VL GPT-5.4 Mini (Low) Full task 30.8 72.4 Interaction specified 33.9 – Reveal performed 81.9 90.4 Naming the interaction changes Qwen3-VL by only 3.1 points, whereas completing it raises accuracy by 51.1 points. Providing the correct reveal-action category is therefore insufficient. Most remaining errors arise from choosing its location or parameters and executing the reveal correctly, before target recognition and final-click localization are evaluated. Target-agnostic heuristics further separate easy and hard reveal patterns (Appendix F.3 ). Fixed scrolling, hovering, and waiting reveal 68.8%, 61.4%, and 87.1% of their matched tasks, whereas popup dismissal and occluder dragging reach 17.6% and 16.9%. The difficult cases require identifying which element controls visibility and how to manipulate it. Failed Qwen3-VL trajectories show the same pattern. When the ground-truth trajectory requires Drag , Scroll , or Move , failed runs omit that action in 59/59, 207/247, and 71/96 cases, respectively (Appendix F.2 ). This motivates first expanding the policy’s action support with SFT, then improving execution with online feedback. 4.4 Learning missing interaction priors We ask whether training can supply reveal actions that base VLMs rarely use. Drag provides the clearest case: Qwen2.5-VL, Qwen3-VL, and GUI-Owl-1.5 emit no drag actions on the held-out tasks. Setup. After excluding two tasks whose ground-truth trajectories could not be replayed reliably, we use 479 tasks for training and reserve 120 for evaluation. The held-out tasks contribute neither SFT examples nor GRPO rollouts. Supervised training on successful trajectories Hu et al. (2022) . We fine-tune the model on human-verified successful trajectories. Let x t x_{t} denote the instruction, screenshot, and interaction history at step t t , and let a t a_{t} be the next ground-truth action. We optimize a weighted next-action negative log-likelihood Pomerleau (1991) : ℒ SFT ​ ( θ ) = − E ( x t , a t ) ∼ 𝒟 ​ [ w ⁡ ( a t ) ​ log ⁡ π θ ​ ( a t ∣ x t ) ] . \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SFT}}(\theta)=-\mathrm{E}_{(x_{t},a_{t})\sim\mathcal{D}}\left[w(a_{t})\log\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid x_{t})\right]. For standard behavior cloning, w ⁡ ( a t ) = 1 w(a_{t})=1 . In the frequency-balanced variant Cui et al. (2019) , we increase w ⁡ ( a t ) w(a_{t}) for rare reveal actions such as Move , Wait , and Drag ; details are in Appendix G . The model still receives goal-only instructions. Only the training distribution changes. Refining interactions with online feedback Shao et al. (2024) . We then apply online GRPO under the same eight-action interaction budget as main evaluation. The reward is defined over browser-executed trajectories rather than text strings: R ⁡ ( τ ) = R out ​ ( τ ) + R proc ​ ( τ ) − λ step ​ | τ | − R err ​ ( τ ) . R(\tau)=R_{\mathrm{out}}(\tau)+R_{\mathrm{proc}}(\tau)-\lambda_{\mathrm{step}}|\tau|-R_{\mathrm{err}}(\tau). R out R_{\mathrm{out}} rewards click-time target success, R proc R_{\mathrm{proc}} gives bounded credit for visibility-changing progress, and R err R_{\mathrm{err}} penalizes wrong clicks, empty clicks, invalid actions, and repeated ineffective actions. Exact weights and optimization hyperparameters are provided in Appendix G . The two stages serve different roles. SFT broadens action support, after which GRPO selects among those actions using online feedback. If a seed policy never samples Drag , GRPO observes no successful drag rollout to reinforce. Frequency-balanced SFT brings rare reveal actions into the policy’s sampled support, enabling GRPO to optimize their selection and execution. Results. The two-stage procedure raises Qwen3-VL from 40.0% to 59.2% GA (Figure 6 ). On Movable Occlusion, frequency-balanced SFT emits Drag in 7/8 required-drag tasks and solves 4/8; GRPO raises this to 5/8. Initialization also matters on Dynamic Target Interaction: GRPO reaches 60.0% from the frequency-balanced seed but 30.0% from the standard SFT seed. The same procedure improves InternVL3.5 from 28.3% to 47.5% and GUI-Owl-1.5 from 35.0% to 52.5% (Table A8 ), showing consistent gains across three architectures. Before comparing models, we therefore verify both with the same 15 participants (protocol details in Appendix H ). Task solvability. Participants solve a fixed suite of 21 tasks, three from each sub-type, using the same instructions and interfaces given to the models, without the constraint label, target ID, target coordinates, or reveal procedure. A trial ends on the correct target click or after eight click-or-drag attempts. Scrolling and hovering are recorded but do not count, so the limit is comparable to, though not identical with, the eight-action model budget. Participants succeed in 298 of 315 trials (94.6%) with a mean completion time of 19.8 seconds (Table 5 ). Together with the replay verification of every reference trace, this indicates that the model failures reported below do not stem from unsolvable tasks or ambiguous instructions. Environment fidelity. The same participants compare seven representative environments with their real-interface counterparts and rate visual realism, interaction realism, and task executability on five-point scales, giving mean scores of 4.50, 4.64, and 4.75 (Table 6 ). Appendix C.2 complements these ratings with visual-similarity metrics and a preliminary paired mock–real evaluation on 16 tasks, one per environment, in which model ordering is preserved across the two settings and the Qwen3-VL model trained in Section 4.4 leads in both. 5 Conclusion We introduced IGG to make visibility recovery a measurable component of GUI grounding. Our analyses show that knowing which interaction is required is not enough; current models most often fail in deciding where and how to carry it out. Training on successful interaction trajectories followed by online feedback improves this capability consistently across model families. IGG therefore provides a focused setting for evaluating and learning the interactions that must precede a grounding click. 6 Limitations IGG uses deterministic mockups for controlled and reproducible evaluation. Our fidelity analyses, including paired mock-real evaluation, suggest that these environments capture relevant visual and interaction patterns, but they do not replace evaluation on live interfaces. Interactive grounding can support accessibility and UI testing, but the same capability may also be misused for automated interaction. We therefore release only controlled mockups that are not connected to external services. C.3 Instruction design Instructions name the target but not the reveal procedure. Annotators avoid action hints such as “scroll down,” “hover over the icon,” or “wait until the button appears,” and add a natural cue, such as an author, document title, or surrounding content, when several elements share a label. For example, “Scroll down and click Kai” becomes “Find Kai in the direct message list,” and “Drag the sticky note away and click QA Checklist” becomes “Click the QA Checklist note without deleting any notes.” Multimodal LLMs propose candidate instructions and reference traces, and annotators correct the wording, repair traces where needed, and replay every task to verify that the target is unique and reachable. Effect of procedural hints. As a diagnostic, we also evaluate instructions that state the intermediate procedure. Unlike the reveal action given condition of Section 4.3 , which names only the action type, these hints describe the procedure. With such hints, Qwen3-VL rises from 30.8% to 56.9% GA over all 601 tasks, but hints do not solve precise manipulation: hinted Qwen3-VL solves 0 of 8 held-out movable-occlusion tasks, whereas SFT+GRPO solves 5 of 8 without any test-time hint. The main benchmark therefore retains goal-only instructions, and the training gains reflect an executable interaction prior rather than instruction following. Appendix G Training Details Our two-stage procedure uses SFT to introduce rare reveal actions and online GRPO to optimize their execution from browser feedback. G.1 Training Setup Two tasks whose ground-truth trajectories could not be replayed reliably during corpus construction are excluded before splitting the remaining 599 tasks into 479 training tasks and 120 held-out validation tasks. Every included ground-truth trajectory is human-corrected and verified by replay; validation tasks contribute neither SFT examples nor GRPO rollouts. G.2 SFT The ground-truth trajectories yield 1,141 action-level examples with normalized coordinates. We use LoRA rank 8, alpha 32, dropout 0.05, all-linear language-model target modules, a frozen vision tower and projector, bf16, learning rate 1 × 10 − 4 1\times 10^{-4} , effective batch size 8, maximum length 8192, maximum image pixels 1,382,400, and 500 steps with checkpoints every 100 steps. Frequency balancing oversamples Click / Scroll / Move / Wait / Drag by 1/1/2/2/4, expanding the data to 1,460 examples and the drag examples from 55 to 220. G.3 Online GRPO GRPO starts from an SFT LoRA seed and collects online browser rollouts from the 479 training tasks under the same eight-action budget used in evaluation. We use group size 6, temperature 1.0, top- p p 0.95 for rollout sampling, learning rate 2 × 10 − 6 2\times 10^{-6} , PPO-style clipping with ϵ = 0.2 \epsilon=0.2 , maximum gradient norm 1.0, and up to 20 update groups. We evaluate saved LoRA checkpoints with greedy decoding on the fixed 120-task validation split. Online interaction reward. The reward is computed from browser-executed traces. Let S S denote target-click success; T T the action count; W W non-empty wrong clicks; E E empty clicks; I I invalid actions; A A repeated ineffective actions; and R R repeated wrong-click locations. The bounded bonus B B rewards reveal progress (Table A9 ). Successful traces with prior wrong clicks are capped at 1.2, shortcut successes at 0.8, and runtime or parsing failures are excluded from policy updates.
